vignette: Rahul had always been a man who prided himself on his ability to stay calm under pressure. As a product manager at a tech firm, he was no stranger to tight deadlines and high-stakes presentations. But that all changed during a business trip to his home country of India five years ago. While traveling through a rural area, Rahul was detained by local authorities and subjected to hours of physical and psychological torture. The experience left him shaken, but it wasn't until he returned to the United States that he began to realize just how profoundly it had affected him. At first, it was small things. He would find himself becoming disoriented in crowded spaces, unable to make sense of the cacophony of sounds around him. Incomprehensible chatter, like the murmurs of a crowd or the din of a busy restaurant, would send his mind racing and leave him feeling dizzy and lightheaded. Sirens, too, had become a source of dread - the sound would instantly transport him back to those dark hours in detention, where every noise seemed to signal another round of questioning. As time went on, Rahul began to develop strategies to avoid these triggers. He started taking longer routes to work to avoid busy streets, and would often eat lunch at his desk rather than venturing out into the crowded break room. But despite these efforts, he couldn't shake the feeling that danger was always lurking just around the corner. He became hyper-vigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of threat - a habit that left him exhausted and on edge. Rahul's wife, Nalini, began to notice the change in him too. She would try to touch him or give him a hug, only to be met with a startled reaction. "I'm just not used to being touched," he would explain, but deep down, he knew it was more than that. The experience of being tortured had left him with a deep-seated mistrust of others - a sense that anyone could turn on him at any moment. At night, Rahul would wake up multiple times, his heart racing as he checked to make sure the doors were locked and the windows were secure. He knew it was irrational - they lived in a safe neighborhood, after all - but he couldn't shake the feeling that something bad was waiting for him just outside. As the months went by, Rahul's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on his relationships and work performance. His team at work would try to schedule meetings during peak hours, only to have him beg off or suggest alternative times. His friends and family grew concerned about his increasing isolation - but Rahul just couldn't seem to shake the feeling that everything was spiraling out of control. One day, as he was working late in the office, a coworker walked by wearing a jacket with a logo from a local law enforcement agency. Rahul's heart skipped a beat as he caught sight of it - for an instant, he was back in that detention cell, surrounded by the uniforms and guns of his tormentors. It was then that Rahul realized just how much his life had shrunk since the torture. He couldn't go out with friends without feeling anxious, couldn't focus at work without getting distracted by every little noise. And through it all, he couldn't shake the sense that there must be something fundamentally wrong with him - that if only he were stronger, or smarter, or better in some way, this wouldn't have happened. Rahul's wife finally convinced him to seek help after a particularly rough night, where he woke up screaming from a nightmare and couldn't calm down for hours. As he sat in the therapist's office, trying to make sense of it all, Rahul realized just how much he had been living in fear - and how desperately he wanted to find a way out.
